summary: This memo specifies two prime-order groups, ristretto255 and decaf448, for building cryptographic protocols safely. ristretto255 can be implemented on Curve25519, so existing implementations can be reused. decaf448 is similarly built on edwards448. It comes from the Crypto Forum Research Group.

eli5.summary: Some math shapes for secret codes have tricky bumps that cause mistakes. These are smoothed versions with no bumps, easier to use correctly.

questions: how do ristretto255 and curve25519 relate
subtitle: Safe prime-order elliptic curve groups for cryptographic protocols.

tldr.problem: Some cryptographic protocols require a group with prime order (where every non-identity element generates the full group), but the most efficient elliptic curves like Curve25519 have non-prime order with cofactors. Using non-prime-order groups requires protocol-specific workarounds that can introduce subtle security bugs.
tldr.mechanism: Ristretto255 and decaf448 are abstract group interfaces built atop Curve25519 and edwards448 respectively. They use mathematical transformations to present a prime-order abstraction, hiding cofactor-related details and encoding/decoding operations that validate and canonicalize group elements.
tldr.outcome: Developers can implement complex protocols more safely by using a prime-order group abstraction without sacrificing the performance benefits of modern Edwards curves. Existing Curve25519 and edwards448 implementations can be extended with a thin layer to provide these groups.

today: RFC 9496 is an Informational RFC from the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) published in December 2023. It has not been obsoleted and represents consensus guidance from the CFRG on safe group construction for cryptographic protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Ristretto255 and decaf448 are prime-order group constructions based on the Decaf and Ristretto techniques. They solve a key abstraction mismatch: Edwards curves like Curve25519 and edwards448 are fast and have complete addition formulas with no exceptional cases, but the group of points on these curves has a cofactor (a small divisor of the group order), making it non-prime-order. This creates security pitfalls.

Many cryptographic protocols, including signatures and key agreements, rely on the assumption that the group is prime-order (cofactor 1). When protocols that assume prime order run on non-prime-order groups, the curve cofactor must be handled through ad-hoc protocol tweaks that are error-prone. The signature scheme Ed25519, for example, has implementation variations in validation behavior that can affect which signatures are valid.

Ristretto and Decaf fix this abstraction mismatch by providing a prime-order group interface that hides the cofactor, allowing existing Edwards curve implementations to be reused. The abstraction layer adds minimal overhead, only in encoding and decoding.
sections.eli5: A math tool can be weird inside but present a simple, safe face to the outside. Ristretto and Decaf build that friendly face on top of fast curves, so protocol builders don't have to worry about the weird parts.

sections.title: The Group Abstraction
sections.content:
The RFC defines an abstract prime-order group interface with two main types: abstract elements and abstract scalars. Operations on these types include decoding (bytes to element), encoding (element to bytes), equality checking, addition, negation, subtraction, scalar multiplication, and a deterministic element derivation function from fixed-length byte strings.

Encoding and decoding are central to the abstraction. When decoding, the implementation validates the input so that only canonical encodings of valid elements are accepted. This avoids explicit invalid-curve checks. When encoding, the implementation guarantees that equivalent representations of the same element always produce identical byte strings. Re-encoding a decoded element always yields the same bytes.

Element derivation is a deterministic function that maps 64-byte strings (for ristretto255) or 112-byte strings (for decaf448) to group elements. If the input is uniformly random, the output is (nearly) a uniformly random group element. This property makes element derivation suitable for hash-based functions like hashing to elliptic curves.
sections.eli5: A group is a set of things you can add together and get another thing. Prime-order means adding the same thing over and over eventually gets you back to the start in exactly the right number of steps—no strange surprises.

sections.title: Implementation on Edwards Curves
sections.content:
Ristretto255 is implemented using Curve25519 (more precisely, the edwards25519 form of the curve). Internally, group elements are represented as points on the Edwards curve using extended homogeneous coordinates (x, y, z, t). Each abstract group element can have multiple equivalent internal representations, but the public interface exposes only the abstract element type, not the curve point.

The ristretto255 group has prime order l = 2^252 + 27742317777372353535851937790883648493. Scalars are integers modulo l, using the same scalar field as Curve25519, so existing Curve25519 scalar arithmetic implementations can be reused.

Decaf448 works similarly using edwards448. It has prime order l = 2^446 - 13818066809895115352007386748515426880336692474882178609894547503885. Both groups expose a canonical generator for interoperability.

The encoding and decoding operations use sophisticated mathematical formulas involving field operations like square roots of ratios. These are carefully constructed so that only canonical encodings pass validation, and encoded then re-encoded elements match exactly.
sections.eli5: Ristretto255 and decaf448 sit on top of existing curve math. They take the raw curve points, apply some transformations to hide the cofactor, and present you with a clean prime-order group.

sections.title: Element Derivation and Mapping
sections.content:
Both ristretto255 and decaf448 define a MAP function that converts 32-byte (ristretto255) or 56-byte (decaf448) strings into group elements. The element derivation function takes longer strings (64-byte or 112-byte) and applies MAP twice, adding the results together.

The MAP function is not pre-image resistant (given an element, you can find byte strings mapping to it), which is useful: combining a cryptographic hash with MAP creates a hash-to-curve function suitable for commitment and signature schemes. This construction is referenced in RFC 9380 (Hashing to Elliptic Curves).
sections.eli5: The mapping function turns random bytes into group elements in a way that's uniform and useful for hashing, like a cryptographic blender that always produces the same consistency.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
Ristretto255 and decaf448 provide prime-order abstractions suitable for safely implementing higher-level protocols. The safety of the abstraction depends on correct implementation. The RFC emphasizes that implementations should expose an opaque type for group elements, not the underlying curve points. Implementations must not expose internal constants or functions, and must construct group elements only via decoding, element derivation, or group operations on valid elements.

All operations are designed to maintain the invariant that an internal representation is always valid. There is no function to test whether an arbitrary curve point is valid; the decoding function either returns a valid internal representation or an error. Invalid states are unrepresentable.

Constant-time operations are crucial for side-channel resistance. The RFC specifies constant-time comparisons and conditional selections that implementations must use for the encoding, decoding, and equality operations.
sections.eli5: The contracts are simple: only create groups the right way, only expose the safe interface, and keep operations free from timing leaks. Break these rules and you break the safety.
